source: KDT8 ch7, ch8, ch10; GG14 ch74

cards.front: How can the contact time of an eye medication on the ocular surface be prolonged?
cards.back: Gels (e.g. pilocarpine 4% gel releasing drug as the polymer erodes), ointments (mineral oil/petrolatum base, used for antibiotics, cycloplegics, miotics), soft contact lenses, collagen shields and nanoparticle carriers. Blocking tear outflow with silicone punctal plugs also extends dwell time.

cards.front: Classify: ocular routes of drug administration
cards.text: Besides {{topical}} drops, drugs can be given by {{subconjunctival}}, {{sub-Tenon's}}, {{peribulbar}} or {{retrobulbar}} injection, or into the eye by {{intracameral}} (anterior chamber) and {{intravitreal}} injection or device; intravitreal delivery bypasses absorption and suits {{endophthalmitis}}, retinitis and age-related macular degeneration.

cards.front: Why can eye-drop preservatives damage the cornea? Name them.
cards.back: Drops and contact lens solutions often contain benzalkonium chloride, chlorobutanol, chelating agents and rarely thimerosal. Benzalkonium chloride can produce a punctate or even toxic ulcerative keratopathy. Most local toxicity of eye drops is hypersensitivity or direct toxicity to cornea, conjunctiva, periocular skin and nasal mucosa.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacokinetics of topically applied ocular drugs

points: Depends on dwell time in the cul-de-sac and tear film, nasolacrimal drainage, binding to tear proteins, local metabolism and diffusion across cornea and conjunctiva
Cornea acts as a fat-water-fat barrier (epithelium, stroma, endothelium): drugs with both lipophilic and hydrophilic character cross best
Penetration rises roughly in proportion to tear-film concentration and increases when the epithelium is breached (ulcer, defect)
Drug collects in aqueous humour, then reaches intraocular tissues and may drain via the trabecular route into the circulation
Melanin binding: alpha-agonist mydriasis is slower in dark irides; melanin acts as a slow-release reservoir
Ocular esterases, oxidoreductases, COMT, MAO and conjugating enzymes are present
Esterases allow ester prodrugs with better corneal entry (latanoprost); loteprednol is inactivated within the eye, limiting systemic effects
Tears dilute the drug; nasolacrimal drainage carries it to the nasal mucosa
Nasal absorption bypasses hepatic first pass, so eye drops can cause significant systemic effects

cards.front: What are the risks of periocular (sub-Tenon's, peribulbar, retrobulbar) injections?
cards.back: Local tissue injury, globe perforation (with direct retinal toxicity), optic nerve trauma, central retinal artery or vein occlusion, extraocular muscle trauma and a prolonged drug effect. They are used for anterior segment infections, posterior uveitis and cystoid macular oedema.

cards.front: Essay: Why eye drops can cause systemic toxicity, and how ocular drug delivery is optimised

points: Topical drops are the commonest route, yet only a small share enters the eye
Tear dilution and nasolacrimal drainage
Cornea is a fat-water-fat barrier; breached epithelium raises penetration
Tear protein binding and local esterase metabolism
Drained drug is absorbed from nasal mucosa and skips hepatic first pass
Example: timolol drops causing bronchospasm and bradycardia
Longer contact time: gels, ointments, collagen shields, soft lenses, nanoparticles
Ester prodrugs (latanoprost, dipivefrine) for corneal entry
Drugs inactivated inside the eye (loteprednol) limit systemic effects
Intraocular or periocular routes bypass the cornea but carry injury risks

cards.front: What is dipivefrine and how does it lower IOP?
cards.back: A prodrug of adrenaline that crosses the cornea well and is hydrolysed there by esterases. The released adrenaline increases uveoscleral outflow, raises trabecular conductivity (beta-2) and reduces aqueous formation (alpha). It still causes ocular burning and is kept for add-on use.

cards.front: What are Rho kinase inhibitors in glaucoma?
cards.back: Netarsudil and ripasudil, the newest antiglaucoma class. Blocking Rho kinase in the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal reduces actin stress fibres and is thought to increase trabecular outflow. They often cause gold-brown corneal deposits (cornea verticillata) and conjunctival hyperaemia. They also promote corneal endothelial cell proliferation after Descemet stripping surgery.

cards.front: Classify: antiglaucoma drugs by mode of action
cards.text: Reduce aqueous secretion: {{beta-blockers}} (timolol), {{alpha-2 agonists}} (brimonidine, apraclonidine) and {{carbonic anhydrase inhibitors}} (dorzolamide, acetazolamide). Increase uveoscleral outflow: {{prostaglandin analogues}} (latanoprost). Increase trabecular outflow: {{miotics}} (pilocarpine) and {{Rho kinase inhibitors}} (netarsudil). Adrenaline/dipivefrine act on all three.

cards.front: Which ocular structure makes aqueous humour, and which receptors there are targeted to lower IOP?
cards.back: The ciliary epithelium secretes aqueous. It carries beta-2 receptors and alpha-2 receptors, so beta-blockers and alpha-2 agonists cut production. Beta-2 relaxation of the ciliary muscle has no meaningful effect on accommodation, which is why beta-blockers leave vision unchanged.

cards.front: How do topical beta-blockers lower intraocular pressure, and what properties suit an ocular beta-blocker?
cards.back: They reduce aqueous formation: beta-2 blockade in the ciliary epithelium down-regulates adenylyl cyclase, with a secondary fall in ocular blood flow. Pupil size, ciliary tone and outflow are unchanged. A good ocular beta-blocker is lipophilic with high ocular capture and has little or no local anaesthetic action (to avoid corneal hypoaesthesia).

cards.front: Why do timolol eye drops cause systemic adverse effects, and how can they be reduced?
cards.back: Drug drains through the nasolacrimal duct and is absorbed from the nasal mucosa, avoiding first-pass metabolism. Results: bronchospasm (even life-threatening in asthma/COPD), bradycardia, worsening heart block and heart failure, especially in the elderly; all systemic beta-blocker contraindications apply. Pressing on the inner canthus for about 5 minutes after instillation limits entry into the duct.

cards.front: Short note: Ocular beta-blockers compared

points: Prototype; non-selective, no local anaesthetic or intrinsic sympathomimetic action
IOP falls 20-35% within 1 h, effect lasts about 12 h; some effect persists 1-2 weeks after stopping, so a missed dose is safe
About 30% of open angle cases need another drug
Beta-1 selective: fewer bronchopulmonary effects
May protect retinal neurones by reducing Ca2+ influx
Less efficacious than timolol because ocular receptors are mainly beta-2; more stinging
Levobunolol: once-daily alternative to timolol
Carteolol and metipranolol
Stinging, redness, dryness, corneal hypoaesthesia, allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, blurred vision

cards.front: Why are topical beta-blockers preferred over miotics in open angle glaucoma?
cards.back: No change in pupil size (no dim vision in dim light or with cataract), no induced myopia, no brow pain from ciliary/iris spasm, no swings in IOP as with pilocarpine, and once or twice daily dosing is enough.

cards.front: Prostaglandin analogues in glaucoma: mechanism, why first choice, and adverse effects?
cards.back: Latanoprost (a PGF2-alpha ester prodrug), travoprost (FP agonist) and bimatoprost (prostamide) mainly increase uveoscleral outflow, with a smaller trabecular effect; efficacy equals timolol and they work in normal-tension glaucoma. Once-daily use and no systemic effects make them first-line. Local effects: irritation, blurring, increased iris pigmentation, longer darker eyelashes, and macular oedema (watch aphakic eyes). Cost is a drawback.

cards.front: Apraclonidine versus brimonidine in glaucoma.
cards.back: Both are alpha-2 agonists that cut aqueous production (Gi, lower cAMP). Apraclonidine is polar, does not enter the brain, causes frequent allergy, mydriasis and lid retraction, and is used only short-term to blunt IOP spikes after laser procedures. Brimonidine is more alpha-2 selective and lipophilic, also increases uveoscleral outflow, causes less allergy, but can cause dry mouth, sedation and mild BP fall; it is used short- or long-term, usually as add-on. Both may cause rebound red eye.

cards.front: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors in glaucoma: topical versus oral.
cards.back: They inhibit carbonic anhydrase II in the ciliary epithelium, reducing bicarbonate and fluid secretion. Dorzolamide and brinzolamide drops lower IOP about 20% (less than timolol), cause stinging, bitter taste and corneal oedema, and are add-on drugs. Oral acetazolamide is used short-term (angle closure, peri-operative); paresthesia, hypokalaemia, acidosis, malaise, depression and kidney stones limit chronic use.

cards.front: Why are miotics now a last resort in open angle glaucoma?
cards.back: Pilocarpine contracts the ciliary muscle, pulling the scleral spur and opening the trabeculae. But it lasts only 4-6 h (6-8 hourly drops with fluctuating IOP), dims vision in poor light, causes accommodative spasm, induced myopia and brow ache, and stronger drops can give sweating, diarrhoea and bronchospasm. It still works in aphakic glaucoma.

cards.front: Why are mitomycin and 5-fluorouracil used in glaucoma surgery?
cards.back: Applied at the trabeculectomy site, they limit post-operative wound healing and scarring so the filtration bleb stays open. The trade-off is thin avascular tissue that can leak, causing hypotony and a higher infection risk.

cards.front: Short note: prostaglandin analogues in glaucoma

points: Increase uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour, lowering intraocular pressure
Latanoprost is an ester that is hydrolysed to an active acid in the cornea
Now preferred first line in open angle glaucoma, above topical beta blockers
Latanoprost 0.005% once daily in the evening; travoprost 0.004%; bimatoprost 0.03%
Ocular smarting and reactive hyperaemia
Fixed combinations exist, for example latanoprost with timolol

cards.front: Short note: alpha-2 agonists in glaucoma

points: Apraclonidine 0.5%: polar clonidine congener that does not cross the blood-brain barrier
Brimonidine 0.15% and 0.2%: has protective effect on retinal neurones independent of IOP
Apraclonidine restricted to short-term control of IOP spikes
Allergic conjunctivitis and follicular reactions are common

cards.front: Short note: Drug treatment of acute angle closure glaucoma

points: Narrow angle and shallow anterior chamber; attack usually triggered by mydriasis
IOP rises rapidly to very high levels; an emergency that can cost sight
IV hypertonic mannitol (or glycerol) to dehydrate the eye; caution in heart or renal failure
IV acetazolamide, then oral
Pilocarpine drops once IOP starts falling (an ischaemic iris will not respond at very high IOP)
Topical timolol; apraclonidine or latanoprost may be added
Drugs only end the attack: laser or surgical iridotomy is the cure

cards.front: Essay: Pharmacotherapy of primary open angle glaucoma

points: Progressive optic nerve damage with field loss; raised IOP is the main modifiable risk
Lowering IOP slows damage even at normal pressure
About 90% leaves by the trabecular route, about 10% by uveoscleral flow
PG analogues
Beta-blockers
Alpha-2 agonists
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
Rho kinase inhibitors
Miotics, adrenaline prodrug
Start with a PG analogue or a beta-blocker
If target not reached: switch or combine both (fixed combinations aid compliance)
Brimonidine or dorzolamide when first-line drugs are contraindicated or as add-on
Miotics and oral acetazolamide last, then laser or surgery
Nasolacrimal occlusion to limit systemic beta-blockade
Watch asthma, COPD, bradycardia, heart block

cards.front: Short note: acute angle closure glaucoma, emergency measures

points: Raised IOP is above 21 mmHg; the attack needs urgent reduction of IOP
Miotic pilocarpine (1-4%) is used to open the angle, instilled frequently at first
Hypertonic mannitol 20%, 1.5-2 g/kg, to lower IOP
Oral acetazolamide 0.25 g every 6-12 hours to reduce aqueous formation
Glycerine 50% may be given as a retention enema

cards.front: Short note: recent advances in glaucoma management

points: Prostaglandin analogues have displaced topical beta blockers as first line in open angle glaucoma
Topical beta blockers remain useful as add-on or in fixed combinations
Dorzolamide 2% twice or thrice daily as add-on to a blocker or PG analogue
Alpha-2 agonists such as brimonidine as add-on
About 30% of open angle glaucoma patients fail to reach target IOP on one drug
Miotics are a last resort because they cause blurred vision and myopia

cards.front: Compare: mydriatic-cycloplegic antimuscarinics
cards.text: Atropine: dilates in 30-40 min, cycloplegia in 1-3 h, effects last {{7-10 days}}. Homatropine: {{10 times}} less potent, mydriasis 1-3 days. Cyclopentolate: onset 30-60 min, lasts about {{a day}}; preferred for cycloplegic refraction. {{Tropicamide}}: quickest (20-40 min) and briefest (3-6 h) but an unreliable cycloplegic.

cards.front: What is the main ocular contraindication to atropinic drugs?
cards.back: A narrow iridocorneal angle: mydriasis can precipitate acute congestive (angle closure) glaucoma. A marked IOP rise is rare in wide angle glaucoma. Conventional systemic doses of atropine have only minor ocular effects.

cards.front: Uses of miotics in ophthalmology apart from glaucoma.
cards.back: Reversing mydriasis after refraction testing; alternating with mydriatics to prevent or break iris adhesions; intra-operative miosis with intracameral acetylcholine or carbachol; and echothiophate for accommodative esotropia.

cards.front: Which drug is used for refraction testing in a child under 5 years, and why?
cards.back: Atropine 1% ointment applied 24 h and again 2 h before testing (cyclopentolate drops are a faster alternative). Children have high ciliary muscle tone, so homatropine and tropicamide give inadequate cycloplegia. Cyclopentolate absorbed via the nasolacrimal duct can cause transient behavioural changes in children.

cards.front: Which mydriatic is preferred for fundoscopy in an elderly patient, and why?
cards.back: Only mydriasis is needed, so phenylephrine (an alpha agonist with no cycloplegia) is preferred, to avoid precipitating or worsening glaucoma; a short-acting antimuscarinic like tropicamide is the alternative, and phenylephrine is often combined with tropicamide for a faster, stronger mydriasis.

cards.front: Why is atropine used in iritis, iridocyclitis and corneal ulcer?
cards.back: Its long mydriatic-cycloplegic action rests the intraocular muscles and relieves their painful spasm, and it has a local anodyne effect on the cornea. Alternating a mydriatic with a miotic prevents adhesions between iris and lens or cornea and can break those already formed; an alpha agonist can also help break posterior synechiae.

cards.front: How does echothiophate help accommodative esotropia?
cards.back: In hyperopic children constant accommodation drives excess convergence. Echothiophate, an irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor, produces miosis and an accommodative lens change, so less accommodative effort and less convergence are needed. A mydriatic is often added to reduce the iris cysts it causes. Being quaternary, it is poorly absorbed.

cards.front: What is the role of low-dose atropine in myopia?
cards.back: Atropine drops at 0.01-0.5% can slow, even reverse, myopia progression in children; the mechanism is unclear. Dose-dependent effects include allergy, dilated pupils needing sunglasses, and loss of accommodation.

cards.front: Which miotic is linked to cataract, and what other ocular side effects do miotics cause?
cards.back: Echothiophate is linked to cataract, along with retinal detachment, iris cysts, pupillary block and punctal stenosis. Miotics in general cause miosis, induced myopia, decreased vision, brow ache and ciliary body spasm.

cards.front: Essay: Choice of mydriatic and cycloplegic for different clinical situations

points: Mydriasis from alpha-1 on the iris radial muscle; cycloplegia needs antimuscarinic block of M3 on the ciliary muscle
Child under 5 for refraction: atropine ointment, since high ciliary tone defeats weaker drugs
Older child or adult refraction: cyclopentolate or tropicamide (tropicamide is an unreliable cycloplegic)
Fundoscopy in the elderly: phenylephrine, with or without tropicamide, no cycloplegia
Iritis and uveitis: atropine or cyclopentolate to rest the muscle, relieve spasm pain and prevent posterior synechiae; phenylephrine helps break synechiae
Narrow angle: mydriasis may precipitate angle-closure glaucoma
Cyclopentolate and atropine absorbed through the nose can cause behavioural or systemic effects in children

cards.front: Name the topical ocular NSAIDs and their uses.
cards.back: Flurbiprofen (prevents intra-operative miosis in cataract surgery), ketorolac (seasonal allergic conjunctivitis; with phenylephrine in irrigation fluid against miosis), diclofenac (post-operative pain and inflammation), ketorolac and diclofenac (post-cataract cystoid macular oedema, pain after refractive surgery), bromfenac and nepafenac (post-cataract pain and inflammation). Rarely they cause sterile corneal melts, mainly in older eyes with surface disease.

cards.front: Which drugs treat allergic conjunctivitis?
cards.back: Mast cell stabilisers: cromolyn (vernal conjunctivitis), lodoxamide, nedocromil. H1 antagonists with mast-cell stabilising action: olopatadine, ketotifen, bepotastine, azelastine, alcaftadine. Epinastine blocks H1 and H2 and stabilises mast cells. Topical steroids for significant allergy; ketorolac for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis.

cards.front: How is dry eye treated pharmacologically?
cards.back: Artificial tears (electrolytes plus viscosity agents such as cellulose polymers, polyvinyl alcohol, PEG, glycerin, dextran), with or without preservative; bland ointments at bedtime; punctal plugs; topical cyclosporine or lifitegrast (blocks LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1) to raise tear production in inflammatory dry eye; doxycycline for blepharitis; autologous serum tears in severe cases.

cards.front: What is cenegermin, and what is it used for in the eye?
cards.back: Recombinant human nerve growth factor given as an ophthalmic solution. It supports corneal innervation and integrity through TrkA and p75 receptors, and is indicated for neurotrophic keratitis, applied 6 times daily for 8 weeks.

cards.front: Short note: Corticosteroids in the eye

points: Topical: dexamethasone, prednisolone, fluorometholone, loteprednol, difluprednate
Implants: fluocinolone and dexamethasone for chronic non-infectious uveitis; intravitreal triamcinolone
Ocular allergy, dry eye, anterior uveitis, post-operative inflammation
Sub-Tenon's or systemic for posterior uveitis; intravitreal for diabetic and cystoid macular oedema
Parenteral then oral taper for optic neuritis
Posterior subcapsular cataract
Secondary open angle glaucoma: marked IOP rise in about 5% without, but up to 90% with, a family history of glaucoma
Worsen herpes simplex, fungal and acanthamoeba keratitis
Loteprednol reduces but does not abolish the IOP risk

cards.front: Why is a topical corticosteroid harmful in herpetic epithelial keratitis but helpful in disciform (endothelial) keratitis?
cards.back: In epithelial keratitis the virus is actively replicating, so immunosuppression worsens infection. Disciform keratitis is mainly an immune-mediated endothelial reaction, so steroids often speed recovery. Steroid-linked risks to remember: raised IOP and glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract and secondary infection.

cards.front: Short note: Choosing between steroid, NSAID, mast-cell stabiliser and antihistamine in the eye

points: Strongest anti-inflammatory; risk of IOP rise, cataract and infection; loteprednol is inactivated in the eye
Avoid in active herpetic epithelial keratitis
Counter intra-operative miosis (flurbiprofen) and cystoid macular oedema, without steroid IOP effects
Cromolyn, lodoxamide, nedocromil prevent mast-cell release (vernal disease)
Olopatadine, ketotifen, azelastine and similar combine H1 block with stabilising action
Artificial tears first; cyclosporine and lifitegrast treat the inflammatory component

cards.front: Which antivirals are used topically in the eye, and which is most toxic to corneal epithelium?
cards.back: Trifluridine, acyclovir and ganciclovir. Trifluridine is the most toxic to the corneal epithelium. Their main uses are viral keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus and retinitis.

cards.front: Which topical ophthalmic antibacterials carry a blood dyscrasia risk, and what is ciprofloxacin's ocular toxicity?
cards.back: Chloramphenicol and sulfacetamide can cause blood dyscrasias. Ciprofloxacin can leave corneal deposits. Erythromycin ointment is used for superficial infections and to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum.

cards.front: What is the only commercially available topical ophthalmic antifungal, and what predisposes to fungal keratitis?
cards.back: Natamycin, a polyene; other antifungals are compounded for topical, intracorneal, intracameral or intravitreal use. Risk factors: trauma, chronic ocular surface disease, contact lens wear and immunosuppression including topical steroids.

cards.front: How is CMV retinitis treated locally, and what is special about the ganciclovir implant?
cards.back: Intravitreal ganciclovir, injected or as an implant, is an alternative to long-term parenteral antivirals. The implant releases drug at a nearly constant (zero-order) rate over a long period rather than as a bolus. No antiviral is indicated for adenoviral conjunctivitis, which is self-limiting.

cards.front: How is bacterial conjunctivitis and keratitis treated?
cards.back: Bacterial conjunctivitis is usually treated empirically with a broad-spectrum topical antibiotic without culture. Small peripheral keratitis gets frequent broad-spectrum drops; severe central keratitis needs corneal scrapings for culture, then hourly round-the-clock topical antibiotics, often specially made fortified drops.

cards.front: Short note: Management of endophthalmitis and infectious keratitis

points: Bacterial or fungal, usually after intraocular surgery or trauma
Prompt vitreous tap then empirical intravitreal antibiotics
Endogenous type: parenteral antibiotics, sometimes vitrectomy
Bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic or spirochetal causes
Severe central bacterial keratitis: corneal scrapings, intensive drops; steroid only judiciously after days of antibiotics
Fungal: natamycin is the only commercial topical antifungal; Acanthamoeba may need oral miltefosine
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir
CMV retinitis: intravitreal ganciclovir injection or zero-order release implant

cards.front: Besides neovascular AMD, which retinal conditions does bevacizumab treat?
cards.back: Macular oedema arising from diabetic retinopathy and from central retinal vein occlusion.

cards.front: Which agents are anti-VEGF drugs for the eye?
cards.back: Pegaptanib (selective VEGF165 antagonist), aflibercept (receptor fusion protein acting as a VEGF-A decoy), bevacizumab (VEGF-A antibody, widely used off-label), ranibizumab (affinity-matured antibody Fab) and brolucizumab (single-chain fragment). VEGF drives new vessel growth, leakiness and inflammation in wet AMD.

cards.front: What is verteporfin and how does it work in wet AMD?
cards.back: A photosensitiser given IV and activated by a non-thermal laser in the choroidal circulation. Free radicals damage vessel walls, causing platelet activation, thrombosis and occlusion of abnormal vessels. Patients must avoid bright light for about 5 days.

cards.front: Short note: Drugs for neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration

points: Pegaptanib: blocks VEGF-165 binding
Aflibercept: VEGFR1/2 fusion protein acting as a decoy receptor for VEGF-A
Bevacizumab: anti-VEGF-A antibody, used off-label first line; ranibizumab: affinity-matured Fab variant
Brolucizumab: single-chain fragment, longer interval but more uveitis
Raised IOP and endophthalmitis after injection
Possible stroke risk with bevacizumab/ranibizumab
IV verteporfin activated by non-thermal laser in choroidal vessels: free radicals occlude new vessels
Photosensitivity: avoid sunlight and bright light for 5 days
Huge price gap between bevacizumab and ranibizumab with similar outcomes fuels cost-effectiveness debate

cards.front: Compare bevacizumab, ranibizumab and brolucizumab as intravitreal anti-VEGF agents.
cards.back: Bevacizumab is the first available full antibody, used off-label and cheap. Ranibizumab is a smaller affinity-matured Fab derived from it, with similar visual outcomes at much higher cost. Brolucizumab is a single-chain fragment with longer duration but higher uveitis incidence. Bevacizumab and ranibizumab raise a cerebrovascular concern.

cards.front: Essay: Pharmacotherapy of wet age-related macular degeneration and retinal vascular disease

points: Wet AMD is a leading cause of blindness; VEGF165 promotes angiogenesis, permeability and inflammation
Pegaptanib, aflibercept, bevacizumab, ranibizumab, brolucizumab given intravitreally
Bevacizumab also treats macular oedema from diabetic retinopathy and central retinal vein occlusion
Verteporfin photodynamic therapy for classic CNV
Ocriplasmin for vitreomacular traction (lens subluxation risk)
Cost versus similar outcomes, cerebrovascular risk, brolucizumab uveitis

cards.front: Complete: ocular toxicity of systemic drugs
cards.text: Topiramate: choroidal effusion with {{angle-closure glaucoma}}. Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine: {{bull's-eye maculopathy}}. Vigabatrin: permanent {{concentric visual field}} loss. Sildenafil: bluish vision via {{PDE6}} inhibition. Ethambutol: {{optic neuropathy}}. Amiodarone: corneal whorls ({{cornea verticillata}}). Minocycline: blue-grey {{sclera}}. Tamoxifen: crystalline maculopathy and {{cataract}}. Rifabutin with clarithromycin/fluconazole: {{uveitis}}.

cards.front: What ocular changes do steroids, phenothiazines and isotretinoin cause?
cards.back: Steroids (inhaled, systemic or ocular): raised IOP, glaucoma and cataract. Chlorpromazine and thioridazine: brown deposits in cornea, conjunctiva and lids that persist after stopping. Isotretinoin: dry eye and severe meibomian gland dysfunction.

cards.front: Which dyes are used in eye examination and for what?
cards.back: Fluorescein (strip or solution) shows corneal and conjunctival epithelial defects and wound leaks, tests nasolacrimal patency, and is used in applanation tonometry and rigid contact lens fitting; fluorexon is used when soft lenses are worn. Rose bengal and lissamine green stain devitalised cells. IV fluorescein or indocyanine green angiography assesses retinal barriers and can cause nausea, pruritus and allergic reactions.

cards.front: How does chloroquine damage the retina?
cards.back: It accumulates in the retinal pigment epithelium, producing a bull's-eye maculopathy with decreased visual acuity. Chronic users need periodic eye exams.

cards.front: Which anaesthetics are used in eye procedures, and which anaesthetic concerns are eye-specific?
cards.back: Topical proparacaine or tetracaine drops and lidocaine gel; intracameral preservative-free lidocaine for cataract surgery; lidocaine and bupivacaine for infiltration and retrobulbar block. Most inhalational agents and CNS depressants lower IOP, but ketamine raises it. In a ruptured globe, avoid drugs that depolarise extraocular muscles, which could expel ocular contents.

cards.front: Short note: Drug-induced ocular toxicity (chloroquine)

points: Chloroquine has high affinity for melanin and binds tightly to ocular pigment tissue
Retinal damage may cause loss of vision
Corneal deposits may affect vision but are reversible on stopping the drug

cards.front: Essay: Ocular adverse effects of systemic drugs

points: Many systemic drugs reach the lens, cornea, retina or optic nerve
Corticosteroids and tamoxifen: cataract; steroids also raise IOP
Topiramate: choroidal effusion with angle-closure glaucoma
Amiodarone: cornea verticillata
Chlorpromazine, thioridazine: brown deposits that persist
Isotretinoin: dry eye and meibomian gland dysfunction
Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine: bull's-eye maculopathy, around 6 years at normal doses, so periodic exams
Vigabatrin: concentric field loss
Sildenafil-type drugs: PDE6 inhibition, bluish vision
Ethambutol and methanol: optic nerve toxicity

cards.front: What is the Draize eye irritation test?
cards.back: A rabbit test in which a test substance is placed in the eye and cornea, conjunctiva and iris are scored for irritation. It is the eye test OECD accepts for regulatory classification of irritant chemicals.

cards.front: Draize test: dose, restraint and observation period
cards.back: 0.5 mL of test substance into the eye; animal restrained for 4 h; redness, swelling, discharge, ulceration, haemorrhage and blindness are monitored for 14 days.

cards.front: Which in vitro methods replace the Draize eye test?
cards.back: Reconstructed human corneal epithelium models (e.g. EpiOcular), the HET-CAM (hen's egg chorioallantoic membrane) test and the 3T3 neutral red uptake assay.

cards.front: Short note: Assessment of ocular toxicity potential of a new chemical entity

points: New molecules must be screened for toxicity potential in animals before human use (Sarkar p251-255)
Ocular irritancy is a regulatory requirement for topical and ophthalmic products
0.5 mL instilled into the eye; restrained 4 h
Score redness, swelling, discharge, ulceration, haemorrhage, blindness
Observe for 14 days; sacrifice and examine pathology at the end
Compare conjunctiva, pupil size, corneal reflex and light reflex before and after dosing (Medhi PMECP p246)
Corneal epithelium models (EpiOcular), HET-CAM and 3T3 NRU assay (Sarkar p286-290; Ghosh PDF p182)
Known ocular ADRs of drug classes guide the study: corneal deposits, retinal toxicity (chloroquine), cataract and glaucoma with steroids (see p2-ocular-037, p2-ocular-042, p2-ocular-044)

cards.front: What is the water drinking test in glaucoma?
cards.back: A provocative test: a water load lowers blood osmotic tension and raises intraocular pressure. A rise above 6 mm Hg suggests glaucoma.

cards.front: What is the venous congestion test in glaucoma?
cards.back: A provocative test in which venous congestion raises intraocular pressure. A rise above 10 mm Hg suggests glaucoma.

cards.front: Normal intraocular pressure and how it is measured
cards.back: Normal range is 16 to 23 mm Hg. It is measured by tonometry, such as applanation or digital tonometry.

cards.front: Short note: Experimental (provocative) methods to produce raised IOP in glaucoma

points: Provoke a rise in IOP and watch how the eye copes under stress
Measure IOP with tonometry; normal 16 to 23 mm Hg
Water load lowers blood osmotic tension, so IOP rises
Rise above 6 mm Hg indicates glaucoma
Venous obstruction raises IOP
Rise above 10 mm Hg indicates glaucoma
Provocative tests above are used for chronic simple (wide angle) glaucoma
